extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and students of natural philosophy / anatomy interested in optics and the design-argument
extracted.subtask_description: A natural-philosophy exposition describing the anatomy of the eye and ear and the optical/physiological conditions required for clear vision and hearing; used to argue design/wisdom of the creator. Contains observational experiments (dark-chamber, convex glass) as demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tunica cornea (transparent membrane)
rubrics_metrics.description: A transparent membrane, such as the clearest horn or glass, that affords a passage to the light (called the Tunica Cornea or horny membrane).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to admit rays of light into the interior of the eye. The text notes that if rays emerging from air meet the same air inside the eye they would diverge and fail to form a distinct image — hence the necessity of a transparent membrane at the surface. (Context: compared to clearest horn or glass.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Aqueous humour qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The aqueous humour is entirely clear and transparent, thicker than air (about the substance of water), and convexly round.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three qualifications (transparent, denser than air, convex) are required so that rays passing from air through the cornea into the cavity will be refracted (inflected) toward each other and proceed to the next refracting surfaces rather than diverging. Called the aqueous or watery humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple refractions required for image formation
rubrics_metrics.description: The rays of light must be refracted repeatedly (the text describes three successive inflections) so that diverging rays from an object are converted into converging rays which meet at a point on the bottom of the eye to form a distinct image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only a single refraction occurred, rays would either not meet or meet too far behind the eye, producing a large, confused image. Demonstrated by dark-chamber and convex-glass experiments: successive refracting bodies (cornea, aqueous, crystalline, vitreous) are required to bend rays to the proper focal point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystalline humour (lens) properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The crystalline humour must be transparent, thicker (denser) than the aqueous humour, convex in some measure, and is more akin to a solid body than a fluid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function: to produce a further refraction that inflects rays a second time so they can meet nearer to the eye. Observational guidance: the crystalline is convex (especially behind) and behaves like a polished spherical glass; removing it and holding it before a candle projects an inverted image (acts as a lens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vitreous humour qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The cavity behind the crystalline is filled with a very clear and bright humour of the consistency of melted glass or (according to others) the white of an egg; it is of a thinner substance than the crystalline humour and is called the vitreous humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Role: being thinner than the crystalline it allows a further (final) bending of rays so they unite at the point on the bottom of the eye. The text emphasizes the vitreous as the medium filling the posterior cavity and participating in the last refraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystalline shaped as a bi-convex lens (microscope analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: For images to be nice and accurate, there should be a transparent body convex on both sides, with the most convex part undermost — qualities found in the crystalline humour (form of a polished spherical glass).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment: holding the crystalline before a candle and paper shows an inverted image like a glass; placing it before the eye with a pin close behind it produces magnified appearances like a microscope. This serves as evidence that the crystalline functions as a lens/microscope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eye interior must be dark (black within)
rubrics_metrics.description: The interior of the eye must be dark in order to represent images as strongly as in a dark chamber; membranes or tunics are in a great measure of a blackish colour for this very purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: the eye is compared to a dark chamber where images are formed on a white paper; a dark interior prevents scattered light from weakening the image. Anti-pattern: a non-dark interior would produce weak or washed-out images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper aperture/pupil proportion (number of rays)
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be an exact proportion for the hole or space (the pupil) through which rays pass so that the number of rays is neither too great nor too small; too few rays make the image weak, too many make it imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration: making a small hole in paper (smaller than pupilla) shows fainter colours; pupils constrict in bright light and dilate in dim light to regulate rays automatically. Anti-patterns: hole too small (image faint), hole too large (image imprecise); the eye regulates pupil size unconsciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodation by altering lens curvature and relative distances
rubrics_metrics.description: To see objects at various distances distinctly, either the roundness (convexity) of one of the humours must be made more or less convex, or the distance between the crystalline humour and the bottom of the eye must be changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms: (a) four external muscles move the eye and can pull the crystalline backward (changing distance to retina); (b) oblique muscles can press the eye to make the aqueous more protuberant (making eye rounder and altering distances); (c) ciliary fibres/processes are posited to change the figure of the crystalline itself (more or less convex). Empirical indicators: strain or pain when forcing accommodation; optical experiments with flatter/more convex glasses show analogous effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric relation for distinct image formation
rubrics_metrics.description: For the image of an object to be distinct, the distance of the object, the curvature (convexity) of the lensing surfaces, and the distance from the lens to the place of collection (the retina/paper) must be in the correct relation; otherwise the collected rays fall before or behind the paper producing confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dark-chamber experiment: with a convex glass, moving the paper nearer or farther demonstrates how image sharpness depends on these relations. Anti-patterns: if object is nearer or farther without adjusting lens curvature or image distance, the image becomes confused.

rubrics_metrics.name: External ear (concha) design to collect sound
rubrics_metrics.description: Two external ears and the hollow concha are positioned/formed to receive and direct sonoriferous air (sound) into the auditory tube; animals and humans turn the ear or cup the hand to aid reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function: the concha and ear orientation gather and guide sound toward the auditory canal. Observational note: many animals turn the ear toward sound sources; humans cup hand behind ear when one ear fails to improve reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ear composition: membranes supported with cartilage (elasticity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The external ear is composed of membranes supported with cartilages, giving it elasticity so it can bend and resume shape — a design balancing softness (would hang over tube) and hardness (would be inconvenient when lying down).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: elastic cartilaginous framework prevents occlusion of auditory orifice and allows resilience; also possibly aids transmission/tremulous motion of sonorous air. Demonstrable by bending the ear and seeing it return to shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auditory (Eustachian) tube structure and lining
rubrics_metrics.description: The auditory tube begins with cartilage at the external part and becomes bony further in; it is lined on the inside with skin or membrane and leads inward from the concha to the tympanic membrane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function: the tube channels sonoriferous air from the external cavity to strike the tympanic membrane. The text notes the tube's composite cartilaginous-then-bony structure as purposeful for its role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tympanic membrane (drum) properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The tympanic membrane is a round, dry, thin, solid and transparent membrane (the drum of the ear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function: sonoriferous air entering the auditory cavity strikes this membrane and sets it into motion, initiating the process of hearing. The text mentions the possibility of a small orifice in the membrane (anecdotal observation: tobacco smoke passing through).
